segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Week 47 Listening: A Community Cooking Class

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Hi, Tom! I heard you joined a cooking class last month. How’s it going?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Hey, Mia. Yes, I did. It’s actually really fun. I was a bit nervous at first because I hadn’t cooked much before, but now I look forward to it every week.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: That’s great. What do you cook there?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Well, last week we made a vegetable curry. It was the first time I’d used so many spices. The teacher, Chef Anna, showed us how to balance the flavours. She said, “Don’t be afraid to taste as you go.” That advice really helped.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Sounds delicious. Is the class big?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Not really. There are only eight students, so we get a lot of attention. Most of them are beginners like me, but one woman, Lisa, has been cooking for years. She often helps others when the teacher is busy.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Nice. Do you have to bring your own ingredients?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: No, everything is provided. The fee covers the ingredients and equipment. We just need to bring an apron and a notebook. Oh, and we have to arrive ten minutes early to set up.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: How long is each session?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Two hours. We start at 6:30 p.m. and finish at 8:30. But last week we finished a bit late because the curry took longer than expected. Chef Anna said it was fine.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: What do you enjoy most?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: I think it’s the friendly atmosphere. Everyone chats and laughs while cooking. Also, I’ve learned to be more patient. Before, I used to rush and make mistakes. Now I take my time and the food tastes better.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Have you made anything at home?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Yes, I tried the curry recipe for my family last weekend. My mum said it was a bit too spicy, so next time I’ll use less chilli. But they liked it overall.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: That’s a good start. Will you continue after this course?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Definitely. The course runs for six weeks, and we’re in week four now. After that, there’s an advanced class, but I think I’ll practise more at home first. Maybe I’ll join the advanced class next term.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Good plan. Oh, one more thing—can anyone join the class?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: You need to be at least 18, and you have to book online. There’s a waiting list, but it’s not too long. Actually, you should try it, Mia. You’d enjoy it.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Maybe I will. Thanks, Tom!

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Community Garden Q&A Session

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for coming to our monthly community garden meeting. I'm Mia, the volunteer coordinator. Today, I'll answer some common questions about the garden. We've had several new members join recently, so I thought it would be useful to go over the basics for everyone, especially since many of you are new to the area and may not know how things work here.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Hi Mia, I'm Tom. I've just moved here. Can you tell me when the garden is open?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Sure, Tom. The garden is open every day from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. But on Sundays, we close at 4 p.m. for maintenance.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Great, thanks. And do I need to pay to join?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes, there's a small annual fee. It's £10 per person, or £15 for a family. That covers seeds and tools.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: Hello, I'm Lisa. I have two kids. Are children allowed to help?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Absolutely! We welcome families. Children under 12 must come with an adult. We also have a special children's plot where they can plant easy vegetables like carrots and beans.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: That's wonderful. What about the rules for using tools?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Good question. You must return all tools to the shed after use. And please clean them before putting them back. We also ask that you don't take tools home.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: I see. Is there a waiting list for plots?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes, currently there is a waiting list of about three months. But you can join our workshops while you wait. They are free for members.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: What kind of workshops do you run?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: We have workshops on composting, pruning, and seed saving. The next one is on composting this Saturday at 10 a.m. in the garden shed.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Do I need to bring anything?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Just gloves and a notebook. We provide all other materials.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: How can I sign up for the workshop?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: You can sign up by sending an email to garden@community.org. Or you can call 555-1234. But email is faster.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Thanks, Mia. One last thing: is there a newsletter?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes, we send out a monthly newsletter with tips and event news. You'll receive it automatically once you become a member.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: Perfect. Thank you for the information.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: You're welcome. I'm glad to help. Let's make our garden grow together!

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Week 47 Listening: Academic Discussion on a Group Project

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good morning, both of you. Thanks for coming. So, how is your group project on urban green spaces going?

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: STUDENT A (Mia): Well, we've collected quite a lot of data already. We interviewed twenty residents last week.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: STUDENT B (Leo): Actually, Mia, it was twenty-two. Two more people joined at the last minute.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Oh right, twenty-two. Sorry. And we also took photos of three parks.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. And what have you found so far?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Most people said they use the park for exercise, but a few mentioned they go there to relax. One person said she goes to meet friends.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Interesting. Have you thought about how you'll present the data?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: We were thinking of using charts, but Leo suggested a table might be clearer for the interview results.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yes, because the numbers are small. A table shows the exact counts.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: That's a reasonable point. But remember, your audience will be your classmates. They might find a chart more engaging. Perhaps you could use both: a chart for the overall trend and a table for details.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: That's a good idea. We'll do that.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Now, what about the literature review? Have you found enough sources?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: We've got five articles, but two of them are quite old—from the 1990s. We're not sure if they're still relevant.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Old sources can still be useful if they provide historical context. But you should also look for more recent studies. Try the university library database; it has a good selection.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Okay, we'll search there. Also, we're struggling with the conclusion. We don't know how to summarise our findings without repeating everything.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: A good conclusion should not introduce new information. Instead, it should highlight the main patterns and maybe suggest one or two areas for further research. For example, you could mention that your sample was small, so future studies could include more participants.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That makes sense. So we could say that while most people use the park for exercise, a larger study might reveal different trends.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Exactly. Now, when is your presentation?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: In two weeks, on the fifteenth.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: And how long will it be?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: About ten minutes, plus five minutes for questions.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. Make sure you practise timing. Also, decide who will speak about which part. Mia, you're good at explaining methods, so perhaps you could cover that. Leo, you could present the findings.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Sure. And we'll both handle the questions.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Perfect. One more thing: have you considered the ethical side? You interviewed people, so you need to ensure their responses are anonymous.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yes, we didn't record names. We used numbers instead.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Excellent. Well, it sounds like you're on track. Keep me updated.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: The Art of the Follow-Up: Extending Answers in Conversation

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a skill that many advanced learners find surprisingly difficult: extending answers in everyday conversation. You might think that once you can speak fluently, keeping a conversation going is easy. But in fact, even C1 speakers sometimes give short answers that stop the dialogue. So let's look at how to give a two-minute answer that feels natural.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, let me explain what I mean by a two-minute answer. It's not about speaking for exactly two minutes. It's about having enough content to keep the other person interested. A good extended answer usually has three parts: a direct answer, a reason, and an example. For instance, if someone asks, "Do you enjoy cooking?" you could say, "Yes, I do. I find it relaxing after work. For example, last night I made a simple pasta dish and it helped me unwind." That's a direct answer, a reason, and an example.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, why do people give short answers? Often, it's because they are nervous or they think the other person is not interested. But in English-speaking cultures, asking follow-up questions is a sign of politeness. So if you give a short answer, the other person might think you don't want to talk. Therefore, extending your answer is a way to show you are friendly and engaged.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Another important point is using narrative tenses. When you give an example, you often need to tell a small story. For example, "Last week, I was walking in the park when I met an old friend. We hadn't seen each other for years, so we stopped and chatted." Here, the past continuous "was walking" sets the scene, and the past perfect "hadn't seen" shows an earlier event. Using these tenses correctly makes your story clear and interesting.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Descriptive clauses also help. Instead of saying "I met a friend," you can say "I met a friend who I hadn't seen since university." The clause "who I hadn't seen since university" adds detail and keeps the listener engaged. Similarly, you can use "which" or "where" to add information about things or places.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, let's talk about reducing basic errors. Common mistakes include using present tense when telling a past story, or forgetting to use articles. For example, saying "I go to park yesterday" instead of "I went to the park yesterday." These errors can distract the listener. So practice your narrative tenses and articles until they become automatic.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: To sum up, extending answers is a skill that requires practice. Use the direct answer, reason, and example structure. Use narrative tenses and descriptive clauses to add detail. And reduce basic errors by practicing regularly. Thank you.
